_note: The handbook's pages (ui/handbook.gd). Ids are fixed in design/plans/mission-1-contracts.md. Every number has a row in research/junior-astronaut/factcheck.md, named in `source`. `icon` (ui/icons) marks the page in the list and stands in for a missing photo; `shows` says what a photo really is (a space station photo is never our base).

pages.title: Light on Mars
lines: Mars pulls 0.38 as hard as Earth.
So you jump almost three times as high.
Things fall more slowly too.
pages.kid: On Mars you are a super jumper!
pages.source: NASA NSSDC Mars fact sheet, factcheck rows 7 and 249

pages.title: Almost no air
lines: Mars air presses with about 6 millibars.
Earth's air presses with 1,013.
Your suit is a tiny spaceship around you.
pages.kid: Outside, never take your helmet off.
pages.source: NASA NSSDC Mars fact sheet, factcheck row 9
pages.shows: A spacesuit in the space station's airlock, 17 February 2019

pages.title: A weak sun
lines: Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth.
It gets 43% of Earth's sunlight.
So power is always short here.
pages.kid: Small sun, small power.
pages.source: NASA NSSDC Mars fact sheet, factcheck row 15
pages.shows: Sunset in Gale crater, seen by Curiosity

pages.title: Cold nights
lines: Gale's nights can drop to minus 100 °C.
A summer afternoon can reach about 16 °C.
The heaters run on power all night.
pages.kid: Brr! Keep the heaters on.
pages.source: NASA/JPL, Curiosity's weather station, factcheck row 10
pages.shows: Curiosity's weather station in Gale crater

pages.title: Dust
lines: Wind drops dust on the solar wings.
Dust takes about 0.2% of your power every sol.
A cleaned panel can make half as much again.
pages.kid: Brush the wings, get more power.
pages.source: Lorenz 2021 and NASA PIA07458, factcheck rows 180 and 181
pages.shows: The InSight lander under dust, 24 April 2022

pages.title: Solar storms
lines: On 20 May 2024 a solar storm hit Mars.
Curiosity measured it: like 30 chest X-rays.
Not deadly, but doses add up.
pages.kid: When the Sun gets angry, hide.
pages.source: NASA/JPL, June 2024, factcheck row 37
pages.shows: Storm specks in Curiosity's camera, 20 May 2024

pages.title: Gale's ancient lake
lines: Billions of years ago, Gale crater held a lake.
The lake had the ingredients life needs.
Nobody has found life on Mars.
pages.kid: A lake was here. Was anyone home? Nobody knows.
pages.source: NASA release 18-050, factcheck row 70
pages.shows: A drawing of the old lake in Gale crater

pages.title: Air in tanks
lines: One person breathes 0.84 kg of oxygen a day.
Two of you need about 52 kg for 30 sols.
All of it came from Earth, in tanks.
pages.kid: Your air is packed, like a lunch box.
pages.source: NASA BVAD 2022, factcheck rows 23, 132 and 163
pages.shows: An oxygen tank packed for the space station, 16 July 2020

pages.title: The air maker
lines: It splits water into oxygen.
1 kg of oxygen costs about 1.1 kg of water.
It needs about 4 kW of power.
pages.kid: It drinks water and power to make air.
pages.source: NASA ECLSS fact sheet 2025 and ICES-2015-115, factcheck rows 74, 101 and 106

pages.title: The garden
lines: Robots planted this lettuce before you landed.
Lettuce takes 33 days to grow.
Plants give vitamins and smiles, not your air.
pages.kid: Salad is a treat, not your oxygen.
pages.source: NASA NTRS 20190028955, factcheck row 29
pages.shows: Lettuce grown on the space station, 2014

pages.title: Seeds for 30 sols
lines: Microgreens are ready in 7 to 18 days.
Radishes take 25 days.
Both are ready before we leave.
pages.kid: Pick seeds that grow fast.
pages.source: NASA BVAD 2022 and NASA TM 2025, factcheck rows 119 and 121

pages.title: Water
lines: Each of you needs 3.2 kg of water a day.
All of it came from Earth.
This short stay recycles none of it.
pages.kid: Every drop came with you.
pages.source: NASA BVAD 2022 and ICES-2023-265, factcheck rows 25 and 132
pages.shows: The space station's water machine, 22 March 2016

pages.title: Solar wings
lines: Solar wings turn sunlight into electricity.
They turn to follow the Sun.
Dust on the glass means less power.
pages.kid: Clean wings fill the battery.
pages.source: NASA NSSDC Mars fact sheet and Lorenz 2021, factcheck rows 15 and 180
pages.shows: Testing InSight's solar panels on Earth, 23 January 2018

pages.title: The reactor
lines: NASA picked fission power for the first Mars crews.
It works day, night and in dust storms.
Ours gives 10 kW.
pages.kid: It never sleeps.
pages.source: NASA Moon to Mars architecture 2024, factcheck rows 21 and 210
pages.shows: Testing a power maker for a small reactor, on Earth

pages.title: The oxygen valve
lines: If the oxygen alarm rings, do not wait for Earth.
Turn the valve beside the air maker.
Earth's answer would come too late.
pages.kid: Alarm? Turn the valve.
pages.source: This base's own rule. The radio delay: factcheck rows 12 and 250

pages.title: The radio
lines: On 14 November 2026 a message takes about 11 minutes each way.
It can take from 3 to 22 minutes.
So an answer comes long after you ask.
pages.kid: Say hello, then wait and wait.
pages.source: JPL orbit tables and NASA NSSDC, factcheck rows 12 and 250
pages.shows: A giant dish on Earth that talks to spacecraft

pages.title: The storm shelter
lines: Water stops radiation better than metal.
About 5 cm of water halves a storm's dose.
A crew can stay inside for up to a day.
pages.kid: Hide behind the water walls.
pages.source: NASA ICES 2013 and NASA Orion, factcheck rows 35, 87 and 90

pages.title: The rover
lines: Apollo crews stayed within about 9.7 km of their lander.
That was how far they could walk back if the rover broke.
Mont Mercou is 8.8 km away.
pages.kid: Never drive farther than you can walk home.
pages.source: NASA SP-350 and our map maths, factcheck rows 232 and 266
pages.shows: An Apollo 17 astronaut on the Moon, December 1972

pages.title: PIP
lines: PIP is your robot helper.
Robots like PIP set up the base before you landed.
PIP always tells you the truth.
pages.kid: A friend on wheels.
pages.source: PIP is made up for this game. NASA plans send robots first: factcheck row 152

pages.title: Mission Control
lines: Real people on Earth watch over the mission.
They can give advice by radio.
They cannot rescue you: Earth is months away.
pages.kid: They help. You decide.
pages.source: NASA Human Research Program, factcheck rows 1 and 13

pages.title: Opportunity
lines: A dust storm was spotted on 30 May 2018.
Opportunity's last signal came on 10 June 2018.
NASA sent over 1,000 commands to wake it.
pages.kid: Dust hid the Sun, and the rover fell asleep.
pages.source: NASA/JPL Opportunity updates, factcheck rows 16 and 18
pages.shows: How dark the storm made the Sun (simulated)

pages.title: InSight
lines: InSight's panels made 5,000 watt-hours a sol at first.
Under dust they made about 500.
Its last contact was on 15 December 2022.
pages.kid: Dusty panels, empty battery.
pages.source: NASA Science 2022, factcheck rows 22 and 160

pages.title: Curiosity
lines: Curiosity is a NASA rover.
It has worked in Gale crater since 2012.
In November 2026 it was still drilling rocks.
pages.kid: An old friend lives in this crater.
pages.source: NASA Curiosity blog, factcheck rows 1 and 228
